stem:
A 52-year-old man noticed a sore on the underside of his penis a week after returning from a holiday where he had sex with a new partner. On examination there is a single clean ulcer with a firm, button-like base that is not tender. There are rubbery, non-tender lymph nodes in both groins. He feels otherwise well.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Genital herpes
options.B: Primary syphilis
options.C: Chancroid
options.D: Behçet's disease
options.E: Fixed drug eruption

correct_answer: B. Primary syphilis
why_correct: Primary syphilis presents with a chancre: typically a single, painless ulcer with an indurated, clean base, appearing around three weeks (range 9 to 90 days) after exposure. It is often accompanied by painless, rubbery regional lymph nodes. Without treatment it heals but the infection progresses to secondary syphilis.
why_wrong: A. Herpes causes multiple painful vesicles and shallow ulcers with tender nodes. C. Chancroid causes painful, ragged ulcers with tender, sometimes suppurating nodes, and is rare in the UK. D. Behçet's causes recurrent painful oral and genital ulcers. E. A fixed drug eruption produces a dusky plaque that recurs at the same site after a drug, not a painless indurated ulcer.
pearl: Remember that painless chancres in the anal canal, rectum or mouth are easily missed, so ask about all sites of sexual contact.
thinking: New sexual partner ↓ Single ulcer that is painless ↓ Indurated clean base ↓ Rubbery, non-tender inguinal nodes ↓ Primary syphilis
exam_trap: A, Genital herpes — it is the commonest cause of genital ulcers in the UK, but herpetic ulcers are painful and multiple, unlike this single indurated chancre.
takeaway: A single painless ulcer with an indurated base is a syphilitic chancre until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman has her third outbreak of genital herpes this year, confirmed by swab when it first occurred. She has been in a faithful relationship for two years and asks whether her partner must be giving it back to her each time.

Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Her partner is reinfecting her at each outbreak
options.B: The virus was fully cleared after the first episode and these are new infections
options.C: The recurrences are due to a secondary bacterial infection of the skin
options.D: The virus lies dormant in sensory nerve ganglia and periodically reactivates
options.E: Small amounts of virus persist permanently on the surface of the skin

correct_answer: D. The virus lies dormant in sensory nerve ganglia and periodically reactivates
why_correct: After primary infection, herpes simplex virus travels along sensory nerves and establishes lifelong latency in the dorsal root (sacral) ganglia. Triggers such as stress, illness or menstruation can cause reactivation, with virus travelling back down the nerve to the skin. Recurrences therefore do not imply a new infection or infidelity, and frequent episodes can be managed with suppressive aciclovir.
why_wrong: A. Reinfection is not needed to explain recurrences, which come from her own latent virus. B. HSV is never cleared after the primary episode. C. Recurrences are viral, not bacterial. E. Between episodes the virus resides in nerve ganglia; asymptomatic shedding occurs intermittently but the reservoir is neural, not the skin surface.
pearl: Recurrent episodes are usually milder and shorter than the first, and often preceded by a prodrome of tingling or burning.
thinking: Recurrent confirmed genital herpes ↓ Worry about reinfection by her partner ↓ HSV establishes latency after primary infection ↓ Reservoir is the sensory ganglia ↓ Reactivation causes recurrences
exam_trap: A, Reinfection by her partner — it seems a logical explanation for repeated episodes, but recurrences come from reactivation of her own latent virus.
takeaway: Herpes simplex remains latent in sensory ganglia for life and recurrences reflect reactivation, not reinfection.

stem:
A 26-year-old man attends the sexual health clinic after two days of tingling on his penis, followed by clusters of small blisters on the shaft that have burst to leave very sore shallow erosions. He feels feverish and achy, passing urine stings, and both groins have tender nodes.

Which organism is most likely responsible?

options.A: Treponema pallidum
options.B: Haemophilus ducreyi
options.C: Human papillomavirus
options.D: Chlamydia trachomatis
options.E: Herpes simplex virus

correct_answer: E. Herpes simplex virus
why_correct: A prodrome of tingling followed by grouped vesicles that break down into painful shallow erosions, with systemic upset and tender inguinal nodes, is typical of a first episode of genital herpes. Most cases in the UK are due to HSV-2 or increasingly HSV-1. A swab for HSV PCR confirms it, and oral aciclovir started within five days shortens the episode.
why_wrong: A. Treponema pallidum causes a single painless chancre, not grouped painful vesicles. B. Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid with deep, ragged painful ulcers, but it is rare in the UK and does not start as vesicles. C. HPV causes painless warts. D. Chlamydia trachomatis usually causes urethritis or is asymptomatic; its LGV serovars cause a transient painless ulcer.
pearl: First episodes are often more severe than recurrences and can cause urinary retention from pain or sacral radiculopathy.
thinking: Prodromal tingling ↓ Grouped vesicles becoming painful erosions ↓ Fever, myalgia and dysuria ↓ Tender inguinal lymphadenopathy ↓ Herpes simplex virus
exam_trap: B, Haemophilus ducreyi — chancroid also causes painful genital ulcers with tender nodes, but it does not begin as grouped vesicles and is rare in the UK.
takeaway: Painful grouped vesicles that break down into shallow genital ulcers are caused by herpes simplex virus.

stem:
A theatre nurse attends the occupational health department two days after blood from an HIV-positive patient splashed into her eye during an emergency laparotomy. She rinsed her eye at the time but did not report the incident until today. The source patient had recently stopped antiretroviral therapy and his viral load is detectable.

What should be offered now?

options.A: Reassurance only, because conjunctival exposure carries no meaningful HIV risk
options.B: Baseline HIV test with a repeat in three months and no further treatment
options.C: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin as the priority intervention
options.D: A 28-day course of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis started as soon as possible today
options.E: No intervention, because the window for any preventive treatment has already passed

correct_answer: D. A 28-day course of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis started as soon as possible today
why_correct: Mucous membrane exposure to blood from a source with a detectable HIV viral load is a recognised indication for post-exposure prophylaxis. PEP works best when started as early as possible, ideally within hours, but it can still be offered up to 72 hours after the exposure. At two days she is still within that window, so a 28-day course should be started today alongside baseline testing and follow-up.
why_wrong: A. Conjunctival splashes do carry a small transmission risk and are an accepted indication for PEP when the source is viraemic. B. Testing alone wastes the chance to prevent infection while she is still within the treatment window. C. Hepatitis B immunoglobulin addresses hepatitis B, not HIV, and the source is known to have HIV. E. PEP can still be started up to 72 hours after exposure, so the window has not closed.
pearl: PEP is not usually recommended when the source patient is on antiretroviral therapy with a confirmed undetectable viral load, because the risk of transmission is negligible.
thinking: Blood splash to a mucous membrane ↓ Source HIV-positive with detectable viral load ↓ Significant exposure, so PEP is indicated ↓ Presenting at 48 hours is still within the 72-hour window ↓ Start a 28-day course today with baseline testing
exam_trap: E, No intervention because the window has passed — the delay in reporting makes it feel too late, but PEP can still be started up to 72 hours after exposure.
takeaway: After a significant HIV exposure, start PEP as soon as possible, and it remains worthwhile up to 72 hours afterwards.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman has a reactive fourth-generation HIV test confirmed at the sexual health clinic. Before discussing treatment and the need for prophylaxis against opportunistic infections, the team wants to know how far her immune system has been damaged.

Which blood test gives this information?

options.A: CD4 lymphocyte count
options.B: Total white cell count
options.C: Serum immunoglobulin levels
options.D: C-reactive protein
options.E: HIV p24 antigen level

correct_answer: A. CD4 lymphocyte count
why_correct: HIV destroys CD4 helper T lymphocytes, so the absolute CD4 count is the standard measure of how immunocompromised a person is. It guides the risk of opportunistic infections and decisions such as starting co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and it is monitored alongside viral load once treatment starts.
why_wrong: B. The total white cell count is too non-specific and can be normal despite a very low CD4 count. C. Immunoglobulins are often raised in HIV and do not reflect cellular immune damage. D. CRP reflects inflammation, not immune competence. E. p24 antigen is useful for early diagnosis but does not measure immune suppression.
pearl: The CD4 count shows immune damage, whereas the HIV viral load shows how well antiretroviral therapy is suppressing the virus.
thinking: Confirmed HIV infection ↓ Question is about degree of immune damage ↓ HIV targets CD4 helper T cells ↓ CD4 count reflects immunosuppression ↓ Viral load is used for treatment response
exam_trap: E, HIV p24 antigen level — it is an HIV-specific test so it seems relevant, but it helps with early diagnosis and does not measure immune damage.
takeaway: The CD4 count is the measure of immune suppression in HIV.

stem:
A 14-year-old boy who has not received any MMR vaccines is brought to the emergency department. A week ago he developed painful swelling of both parotid glands, and over the last day he has had a worsening headache, has vomited several times and finds bright light uncomfortable. He is alert, his neck is stiff on flexion and there is no rash.

Which complication is most likely?

options.A: Bacterial parotitis spreading to the deep neck
options.B: Acute pancreatitis
options.C: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
options.D: Mumps orchitis
options.E: Aseptic (viral) meningitis

correct_answer: E. Aseptic (viral) meningitis
why_correct: Mumps virus commonly invades the central nervous system, and aseptic meningitis is one of its most frequent complications, usually appearing within about a week or so of the parotitis, although it can occur before or without parotid swelling. Headache, vomiting, photophobia and neck stiffness in an alert, unvaccinated teenager with recent bilateral parotid swelling fit this well. The illness is usually self-limiting, but bacterial meningitis must still be considered and excluded.
why_wrong: A. Deep neck infection would cause neck swelling, trismus and systemic toxicity rather than meningism. B. Pancreatitis causes upper abdominal pain and vomiting but not photophobia or neck stiffness. C. Subarachnoid haemorrhage has a sudden thunderclap onset and is not linked to mumps. D. Orchitis causes a painful swollen testis, not headache and meningism.
pearl: Mumps is a notifiable disease in the UK, and outbreaks still occur in teenagers and young adults who missed one or both MMR doses.
thinking: Unvaccinated teenager ↓ Bilateral parotitis a week ago ↓ Now headache, vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness ↓ Alert with no rash ↓ Mumps aseptic meningitis
exam_trap: D, Mumps orchitis — it is the best-known complication of mumps in males, but it causes testicular pain and swelling, not meningism.
takeaway: Meningism a few days after mumps parotitis suggests aseptic viral meningitis.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct: softened timing of mumps meningitis (within about a week of parotitis; can precede or occur without it)

presentation: Blood cultures in suspected bacterial meningitis
stem:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with a high fever, intense headache and neck stiffness that came on over the last 12 hours. Bacterial meningitis is suspected. She is conscious, her airway is safe and she has no rash.

Which investigation should be taken without delay as part of her first assessment?

options.A: MRI scan of the brain
options.B: Throat swab for viral PCR only
options.C: Electroencephalogram
options.D: Blood cultures
options.E: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate

correct_answer: D. Blood cultures
why_correct: In suspected bacterial meningitis, blood cultures should be taken promptly, ideally before the first dose of antibiotics, because they often identify the organism even when a lumbar puncture is delayed or done after treatment has started. Taking them must not hold up antibiotics. Lumbar puncture, glucose, lactate and meningococcal and pneumococcal PCR are also part of the work-up when safe.
why_wrong: A. MRI is not part of the initial assessment and would delay care. B. A throat swab for viruses alone would not identify the bacterial cause. C. An EEG is not needed unless seizure activity is suspected. E. ESR is non-specific and does not influence immediate management.
pearl: If antibiotics have already been given before a lumbar puncture, blood and CSF PCR for meningococcus and pneumococcus can still confirm the cause.
thinking: Fever, headache and neck stiffness ↓ Suspected bacterial meningitis ↓ Need to identify the organism ↓ Take blood cultures promptly ↓ Do not delay antibiotics while sampling
exam_trap: A, MRI scan of the brain — brain imaging feels thorough for a neurological illness, but it is not a first-line test and would delay treatment.
takeaway: Take blood cultures promptly in suspected bacterial meningitis, without delaying antibiotics.

stem:
A 26-year-old man is reviewed on the acute medical unit with two days of headache, dislike of bright light and pain on bending his neck forward. He is orientated, his blood pressure and heart rate are normal, and there are no focal signs. A lumbar puncture is performed. The CSF is clear, with a raised white cell count made up mainly of lymphocytes, a normal glucose ratio and a mildly raised protein.

Which diagnosis best fits these findings?

options.A: Viral meningitis
options.B: Bacterial meningitis
options.C: Tuberculous meningitis
options.D: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
options.E: Migraine with meningism

correct_answer: A. Viral meningitis
why_correct: Clear CSF with a lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose and only a slightly raised protein is the typical pattern of viral meningitis. Combined with a well, orientated young man with stable observations, this is the best fit. Enteroviruses are the most frequent cause in the UK.
why_wrong: B. Bacterial meningitis usually gives turbid CSF with neutrophils, low glucose and high protein. C. Tuberculous meningitis has lymphocytes but a markedly low glucose and very high protein, often with a subacute course. D. Subarachnoid haemorrhage causes a thunderclap headache and blood or xanthochromia in the CSF. E. Migraine does not produce a CSF pleocytosis.
pearl: Partially treated bacterial meningitis can shift the CSF towards lymphocytes, so a history of recent antibiotics makes the CSF harder to interpret.
thinking: Meningism in a well young adult ↓ Clear CSF ↓ Lymphocytes predominate ↓ Normal glucose, slightly raised protein ↓ Viral meningitis
exam_trap: C, Tuberculous meningitis — it also gives a lymphocytic CSF, but the glucose would be low and the protein very high, which is not the case here.
takeaway: Lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose points to viral meningitis.

stem:
A 52-year-old man is admitted with fever, headache and neck stiffness. Over the last hour his GCS has fallen, he has had a seizure and his pupils react sluggishly. The registrar suspects bacterial meningitis complicated by raised intracranial pressure.

What is the correct approach to lumbar puncture and antibiotics?

options.A: Perform a lumbar puncture at once so that CSF is obtained before any antibiotics
options.B: Arrange a CT head and give antibiotics only once the scan has been reported
options.C: Give oral antibiotics and repeat the neurological assessment in four hours
options.D: Withhold all treatment until a neurologist has examined him
options.E: Give intravenous antibiotics immediately and postpone lumbar puncture until it is safe

correct_answer: E. Give intravenous antibiotics immediately and postpone lumbar puncture until it is safe
why_correct: Signs of raised intracranial pressure, such as a falling GCS, seizures and abnormal pupils, are contraindications to an immediate lumbar puncture because of the risk of coning. The lumbar puncture should be delayed until it is safe, but antibiotic treatment must never wait for investigations. Intravenous antibiotics should be given straight away, with blood cultures taken first if this causes no delay, and senior and critical care input sought.
why_wrong: A. Lumbar puncture with raised intracranial pressure risks brain herniation and should not be done now. B. A CT scan may be needed but antibiotics must not be held back while it is arranged or reported. C. Oral antibiotics are inadequate for bacterial meningitis and waiting is dangerous. D. Delaying treatment for a specialist review risks death and disability.
pearl: A normal CT head does not exclude raised intracranial pressure, so a clinical judgement about safety is still needed before lumbar puncture.
thinking: Suspected bacterial meningitis ↓ Falling GCS, seizure and sluggish pupils ↓ Raised intracranial pressure, so lumbar puncture unsafe now ↓ Investigations must not delay treatment ↓ Give IV antibiotics immediately and defer lumbar puncture
exam_trap: B, Arrange a CT head and wait for the report before antibiotics — scanning seems safe and logical, but every hour of delay in antibiotics worsens the outcome.
takeaway: Never delay antibiotics in suspected meningitis; defer lumbar puncture if raised intracranial pressure makes it unsafe.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman who stopped her antiretroviral therapy two years ago is brought in by her sister. For the past three weeks she has had a slowly worsening headache, low-grade fevers and, more recently, episodes of confusion. Her last CD4 count was very low. There is minimal neck stiffness and no focal weakness.

Which opportunistic infection should be considered first?

options.A: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
options.B: Cytomegalovirus retinitis
options.C: Cryptococcal meningitis
options.D: Oesophageal candidiasis
options.E: Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex

correct_answer: C. Cryptococcal meningitis
why_correct: Cryptococcus neoformans causes a subacute meningitis in people with advanced HIV, typically with a headache that builds over weeks, fever and altered mental state, often with little meningism. Raised intracranial pressure is common. The diagnosis is made with serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen, and the opening pressure should be measured at lumbar puncture.
why_wrong: A. Pneumocystis pneumonia presents with exertional breathlessness, dry cough and hypoxia rather than headache and confusion. B. CMV retinitis causes floaters and visual loss. D. Oesophageal candidiasis causes painful swallowing. E. Disseminated MAC causes fever, weight loss, diarrhoea and anaemia rather than a meningitic picture.
pearl: Raised CSF opening pressure is common in cryptococcal meningitis and repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures may be needed to relieve it.
thinking: Untreated HIV with a very low CD4 count ↓ Headache building over weeks ↓ Fever and confusion with little meningism ↓ Subacute fungal meningitis ↓ Cryptococcal meningitis
exam_trap: E, Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex — it also occurs at very low CD4 counts with fever, but it does not usually cause headache and confusion.
takeaway: A subacute headache with fever and confusion in advanced HIV suggests cryptococcal meningitis.

stem:
In late summer, a 22-year-old woman attends the GP surgery with a three-day history of fever, a frontal headache and discomfort looking at light. Her younger brother had a similar illness last week. She is alert, has no rash and no focal signs, and is later confirmed to have viral meningitis.

Which group of viruses is the most common cause in the UK?

options.A: Herpes simplex virus type 1
options.B: Epstein-Barr virus
options.C: Enteroviruses
options.D: Influenza viruses
options.E: Rabies virus

correct_answer: C. Enteroviruses
why_correct: Enteroviruses, such as echoviruses and coxsackieviruses, are the most frequent cause of viral meningitis in the UK. They are spread by the faecal-oral and respiratory routes, cluster in families and peak in summer and autumn. Most cases resolve with supportive care.
why_wrong: A. Herpes simplex type 1 is the classic cause of encephalitis rather than common viral meningitis; type 2 more often causes meningitis. B. Epstein-Barr virus rarely causes meningitis. D. Influenza is not a common cause of meningitis. E. Rabies causes a fatal encephalitis, not meningitis, and classical rabies is not acquired in the UK.
pearl: Viral meningitis caused by herpes simplex type 2 can recur, a pattern sometimes called Mollaret meningitis.
thinking: Fever, headache, photophobia in an alert young adult ↓ Confirmed viral meningitis ↓ Late summer timing and a sick sibling ↓ Common seasonal, family-clustering viruses ↓ Enteroviruses
exam_trap: A, Herpes simplex virus type 1 — herpes viruses are linked with CNS infection, but HSV-1 is the typical cause of encephalitis, not of common viral meningitis.
takeaway: Enteroviruses are the most common cause of viral meningitis.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_wrong E: rabies causes encephalitis not meningitis; 'classical rabies' not acquired in UK (bat lyssavirus exists)

stem:
On a surgical ward, a 79-year-old man who is on day six of intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam for a chest infection that has now clinically resolved develops five episodes of watery, offensive diarrhoea in a day. He is also taking a proton pump inhibitor. Clostridioides difficile infection is suspected and a stool sample has been sent.

Alongside moving him to a side room, which step is most important?

options.A: Start loperamide to reduce stool frequency
options.B: Switch him to oral co-amoxiclav to finish a full ten days
options.C: Stop the broad-spectrum antibiotic and review other contributing drugs such as the proton pump inhibitor
options.D: Delay any change in treatment until the toxin result is back
options.E: Increase the dose of the proton pump inhibitor to protect the gut

correct_answer: C. Stop the broad-spectrum antibiotic and review other contributing drugs such as the proton pump inhibitor
why_correct: Broad-spectrum antibiotics are the main driver of C. difficile infection, so stopping any that are no longer needed is a key part of management. His chest infection has resolved, so the piperacillin with tazobactam can be stopped. Proton pump inhibitors increase the risk and should be reviewed, and isolation with enteric precautions protects other patients while treatment is started according to severity.
why_wrong: A. Antimotility drugs should be avoided because they may worsen toxin-mediated colitis. B. Swapping to another broad-spectrum antibiotic continues the risk. D. Isolation and antibiotic review should start on suspicion, not wait for results. E. Acid suppression increases the risk, so it should be reviewed rather than increased.
pearl: Oral vancomycin is the first-line treatment for a first episode of C. difficile infection in NICE guidance, with fidaxomicin as second line.
thinking: Diarrhoea while on broad-spectrum antibiotics ↓ Suspected C. difficile ↓ Isolate with enteric precautions ↓ Stop unnecessary antibiotics ↓ Review acid suppression
exam_trap: D, Delay changes until the toxin result is back — waiting for proof feels prudent, but antibiotic review and isolation should begin as soon as the infection is suspected.
takeaway: In suspected C. difficile infection, isolate the patient and stop any antibiotics that are no longer needed.

stem:
A healthcare assistant on an elderly care ward asks the infection prevention nurse why the routine is different for a 71-year-old woman with suspected Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea who has been moved to a single room.

Which set of measures is correct for this patient?

options.A: Alcohol hand rub after each contact and standard detergent cleaning of her room
options.B: Gloves and aprons, washing hands with soap and water, and chlorine-based or other sporicidal cleaning
options.C: An FFP3 respirator for all staff entering the room
options.D: Return to the open bay once antibiotic treatment has begun
options.E: A shared commode wiped with alcohol wipes between patients

correct_answer: B. Gloves and aprons, washing hands with soap and water, and chlorine-based or other sporicidal cleaning
why_correct: C. difficile forms spores that resist alcohol and ordinary detergents and survive for long periods on surfaces. Hands must therefore be washed with soap and water to remove spores physically, gloves and aprons are worn for contact, and the environment and equipment are cleaned with chlorine-based or other sporicidal agents. Dedicated equipment and a single room with its own toilet reduce spread.
why_wrong: A. Alcohol hand rub and detergent do not kill spores. C. C. difficile is not an airborne infection, so a respirator is unnecessary. D. Isolation continues until the patient has had no diarrhoea for at least 48 hours, not just until treatment starts. E. Shared equipment spreads spores and alcohol wipes do not remove them.
pearl: Patients remain in isolation until they have been free of diarrhoea for at least 48 hours with a normal stool pattern.
thinking: Suspected C. difficile ↓ Spore-forming organism ↓ Spores resist alcohol and detergent ↓ Soap and water handwashing ↓ Sporicidal cleaning and contact precautions
exam_trap: A, Alcohol hand rub and detergent cleaning — this is standard practice for most infections, but it does not kill C. difficile spores.
takeaway: C. difficile spores need soap-and-water handwashing and sporicidal cleaning, not alcohol gel.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman in a care home is admitted to a medical ward with three days of loose, foul-smelling stools after a recent course of clindamycin for cellulitis. A stool sample has gone to the laboratory and the result is expected tomorrow. The ward has a free side room with its own toilet.

What should happen now?

options.A: Keep her in the open bay until a positive toxin result confirms the infection
options.B: Place her in a bay with other patients who have diarrhoea, sharing one toilet
options.C: Give loperamide and keep her in the open bay if the diarrhoea settles
options.D: Move her to the side room now with contact precautions, and assess and treat her
options.E: Transfer her to another ward to protect the current ward

correct_answer: D. Move her to the side room now with contact precautions, and assess and treat her
why_correct: Isolation and contact precautions should begin as soon as C. difficile infection is suspected, not after laboratory confirmation, because spores spread rapidly in a shared environment. A recent course of clindamycin with new offensive diarrhoea makes the diagnosis likely. She should be moved to the side room with its own toilet, assessed for severity and treated, with her medicines reviewed.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for the result allows spores to contaminate the bay in the meantime. B. Cohorting with other patients with undiagnosed diarrhoea risks cross-infection. C. Antimotility drugs are avoided and she still needs isolation. E. Moving her to another ward spreads the risk rather than containing it.
pearl: Clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav and quinolones carry a particularly high risk of C. difficile infection.
thinking: Recent clindamycin ↓ New offensive diarrhoea ↓ Suspected C. difficile ↓ Isolate on suspicion, not on result ↓ Side room with contact precautions, assess and treat
exam_trap: A, Keep her in the open bay until the result — it avoids using a side room unnecessarily, but spores can spread widely during that time.
takeaway: Isolate on suspicion of C. difficile infection; do not wait for the toxin result.

stem:
The practice nurse is planning a recall campaign for the routine shingles (herpes zoster) vaccine at a GP surgery. She checks which patients the NHS routine programme is aimed at.

Which group is it mainly designed to protect?

options.A: Infants at their eight-week immunisations
options.B: Healthy adolescents in secondary school
options.C: Healthcare workers with no history of chickenpox
options.D: Pregnant women in the third trimester
options.E: Older adults, in whom shingles and its complications become more common and severe

correct_answer: E. Older adults, in whom shingles and its complications become more common and severe
why_correct: Reactivation of varicella zoster virus becomes more frequent with age as cell-mediated immunity declines, and older people have the highest rates of shingles and post-herpetic neuralgia. The UK routine shingles programme therefore offers vaccination to older adults at specified ages, with additional eligibility for people who are severely immunosuppressed.
why_wrong: A. Infants are not offered shingles vaccine; their routine schedule covers other infections. B. Adolescents are offered vaccines such as HPV and MenACWY, not shingles vaccine. C. Non-immune healthcare workers are offered varicella (chickenpox) vaccine, which is different. D. Pregnant women are offered pertussis and RSV vaccines, not shingles vaccine.
pearl: The non-live recombinant shingles vaccine (Shingrix) can be given to immunosuppressed people, who cannot receive live vaccines.
thinking: Shingles is reactivation of varicella zoster virus ↓ Cell-mediated immunity wanes with age ↓ Incidence and post-herpetic neuralgia rise in older people ↓ Programme targets older adults ↓ Immunosuppressed people also eligible
exam_trap: C, Healthcare workers with no history of chickenpox — they are offered a varicella-related vaccine, but it is chickenpox vaccine, not shingles vaccine.
takeaway: The UK shingles programme targets older adults because shingles risk rises with age.

stem:
A 32-year-old man on high-dose oral corticosteroids for a flare of an autoimmune condition asks his GP which of his outstanding vaccines must be postponed because it contains weakened live virus.

Which vaccine is this?

options.A: Tetanus, diphtheria and polio booster
options.B: Hepatitis B vaccine
options.C: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine
options.D: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine
options.E: Inactivated influenza injection

correct_answer: D. Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine
why_correct: MMR contains live attenuated measles, mumps and rubella viruses. Live vaccines can cause disseminated infection in significantly immunosuppressed people, such as those on high-dose systemic corticosteroids, so they should be postponed until the immune system has recovered. The other vaccines listed are inactivated, toxoid, subunit or polysaccharide preparations and are safe, though they may work less well.
why_wrong: A. The tetanus, diphtheria and polio booster contains toxoids and inactivated polio virus. B. Hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant surface antigen vaccine. C. The pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is non-live. E. The injectable influenza vaccine is inactivated.
pearl: Other live vaccines used in the UK include BCG, oral rotavirus, yellow fever, varicella and the intranasal influenza vaccine for children.
thinking: Immunosuppressed by high-dose steroids ↓ Live vaccines risk vaccine-strain infection ↓ Identify the live attenuated vaccine ↓ MMR contains live viruses ↓ Postpone MMR
exam_trap: E, Inactivated influenza injection — some flu vaccines are live, but that is the children's nasal spray; the injection is inactivated.
takeaway: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine and should be avoided in significant immunosuppression.

stem:
At her booking visit, a 27-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant tells the midwife that she missed her second MMR dose as a child and asks whether she can have it now. Her rubella immunity is uncertain.

What is the correct advice?

options.A: Give it now, because rubella immunity is most important during pregnancy
options.B: Advise that all vaccines must be avoided until after delivery
options.C: Give it in the second trimester once organogenesis is complete
options.D: Postpone MMR until after the birth, because live vaccines are generally avoided in pregnancy
options.E: Advise termination of pregnancy if she has already been given MMR

correct_answer: D. Postpone MMR until after the birth, because live vaccines are generally avoided in pregnancy
why_correct: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine, and live vaccines are generally avoided during pregnancy because of a theoretical risk to the fetus. She should be offered MMR after delivery, and advised to avoid contact with rash illnesses and to report any exposure. Inactivated vaccines such as pertussis, influenza and RSV are recommended in pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. Although rubella protection matters, live vaccines are not given in pregnancy. B. Several inactivated vaccines are actively recommended in pregnancy. C. There is no safe trimester for routine live vaccination. E. Inadvertent MMR in pregnancy has not been shown to harm the fetus and is not a reason for termination.
pearl: Women given MMR are advised to avoid becoming pregnant for one month afterwards.
thinking: Pregnant woman asking about MMR ↓ MMR is live attenuated ↓ Live vaccines generally avoided in pregnancy ↓ Inactivated vaccines remain recommended ↓ Offer MMR after delivery
exam_trap: B, All vaccines must be avoided until after delivery — it seems cautious, but pertussis, influenza and RSV vaccines are recommended in pregnancy.
takeaway: Live vaccines such as MMR are generally postponed until after pregnancy.

presentation: Anaphylaxis to a previous vaccine dose
stem:
The mother of a 4-month-old girl brings her for the next dose of a routine vaccine. The records show that minutes after the previous dose of the same vaccine the baby developed widespread hives, wheeze and floppiness, and was treated with intramuscular adrenaline in the surgery.

What is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Give the dose today and observe her in the waiting room for 15 minutes
options.B: Give it after a dose of oral chlorphenamine
options.C: Do not give further doses of this vaccine until specialist advice has been obtained
options.D: Split the dose into two halves given 30 minutes apart
options.E: Give the dose with a short course of oral prednisolone

correct_answer: C. Do not give further doses of this vaccine until specialist advice has been obtained
why_correct: A confirmed anaphylactic reaction to a previous dose of a vaccine, or to one of its components, is a contraindication to further doses of the same vaccine. Hives, wheeze and collapse treated with adrenaline is anaphylaxis. The vaccine should be withheld and specialist advice sought, for example from an immunologist or paediatric allergy service, about safer alternatives or supervised vaccination.
why_wrong: A. Routine observation does not make it safe to repeat a vaccine that caused anaphylaxis. B. Antihistamine premedication does not prevent anaphylaxis and may mask early signs. D. Splitting the dose is not an accepted approach and still exposes her to the trigger. E. Steroid cover does not prevent anaphylaxis.
pearl: Minor local reactions, mild fever, family history of allergy and egg allergy are generally not contraindications to routine vaccines.
thinking: Previous dose caused hives, wheeze and collapse ↓ Treated with adrenaline, so anaphylaxis ↓ Anaphylaxis to the same vaccine is a contraindication ↓ Withhold the dose ↓ Seek specialist advice
exam_trap: B, Give it after oral chlorphenamine — premedication sounds protective, but it does not prevent anaphylaxis and is not recommended.
takeaway: Do not repeat a vaccine that caused anaphylaxis without specialist assessment.

stem:
A father asks the health visitor how his 6-week-old son can be protected from measles when he is too young to receive the MMR vaccine. She explains that because most children and adults around him are immune, the baby is less likely to meet the virus.

Which mechanism underlies this protection?

options.A: Antibodies from vaccinated people pass to nearby infants through close contact
options.B: Vaccination of others makes the measles virus less virulent
options.C: A high rate of vaccination eliminates the need for the baby to be immunised later
options.D: Fewer susceptible people means chains of transmission are interrupted
options.E: Vaccinated people shed vaccine virus that immunises the baby

correct_answer: D. Fewer susceptible people means chains of transmission are interrupted
why_correct: When a high proportion of a population is immune, an infected person meets fewer susceptible contacts, so each case generates fewer new cases and chains of transmission break. This indirect protection, known as herd immunity, shields people who cannot be vaccinated, such as young infants or the severely immunosuppressed. Measles is highly infectious, so very high coverage is needed to maintain it.
why_wrong: A. Antibodies are not transferred between people by contact; infants receive some maternal antibody only across the placenta and in breast milk. B. Vaccinating others does not change the virulence of the virus. C. The baby still needs MMR at the scheduled ages, as herd protection is incomplete. E. MMR vaccine virus is not shed in a way that immunises contacts.
pearl: The more infectious a disease, the higher the vaccination coverage needed to achieve herd immunity, which is why measles needs around 95 percent uptake.
thinking: Infant too young for MMR ↓ Most people around him are immune ↓ Infected people meet fewer susceptible contacts ↓ Transmission chains are interrupted ↓ Indirect protection of the unvaccinated
exam_trap: C, High vaccination rates remove the need to immunise the baby later — herd protection feels reassuring, but it is incomplete and he still needs his own MMR doses.
takeaway: High vaccine coverage protects unvaccinated people by interrupting transmission.

stem:
A 45-year-old man who works as a bus driver is diagnosed with sputum smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis after months of cough and weight loss. His wife, who shares his bedroom, is referred to the TB service for contact screening.

By which route is she most likely to have been exposed?

options.A: Contact with his blood
options.B: Sexual contact
options.C: Sharing cutlery and food
options.D: Inhaling airborne droplet nuclei from his coughing
options.E: Insect bites

correct_answer: D. Inhaling airborne droplet nuclei from his coughing
why_correct: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is spread by the airborne route: a person with infectious pulmonary disease releases tiny droplet nuclei when coughing, speaking or sneezing, and these remain suspended and are inhaled by others. Prolonged close contact in an enclosed space, such as sharing a bedroom, carries the highest risk, which is why household contacts are screened.
why_wrong: A. TB is not a blood-borne infection. B. Sexual contact is not the transmission route, although close household contact is the risk. C. Sharing cutlery and food does not spread pulmonary TB. E. TB has no insect vector.
pearl: Patients with infectious pulmonary TB in hospital should be nursed in a single room, and those with suspected multidrug-resistant disease in a negative-pressure room.
thinking: Smear-positive pulmonary TB ↓ Bacilli released when coughing ↓ Droplet nuclei stay suspended in air ↓ Inhaled by close contacts ↓ Airborne transmission
exam_trap: C, Sharing cutlery and food — close household sharing is linked to risk, but it is the shared air, not the utensils, that transmits TB.
takeaway: Pulmonary tuberculosis is spread by the airborne route.

stem:
A healthcare assistant on an orthopaedic ward has just helped a 79-year-old woman, recently treated with clindamycin, to use the commode after several episodes of loose, offensive stool. A stool sample has been sent for Clostridioides difficile testing.

After removing her gloves and apron, how should she clean her hands?

options.A: Rub her hands with alcohol-based gel at the bedside
options.B: Wash her hands with liquid soap and running water
options.C: Use an antiseptic hand wipe without washing
options.D: No further hand cleaning is needed because gloves were worn
options.E: Rinse her hands under the tap without soap

correct_answer: B. Wash her hands with liquid soap and running water
why_correct: C. difficile forms spores that are not killed by alcohol, so alcohol gel leaves them on the skin. Washing with soap and running water physically removes spores through friction and rinsing. This applies whenever C. difficile is suspected, not only once it is confirmed.
why_wrong: A. Alcohol gel does not kill or reliably remove C. difficile spores. C. Antiseptic wipes do not replace the mechanical removal achieved by proper handwashing. D. Gloves can have defects and hands become contaminated on removal, so hand hygiene is still needed. E. Water alone without soap is ineffective at removing spores.
pearl: Prior antibiotics, particularly clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav and quinolones, are the main risk factor for C. difficile infection.
thinking: Diarrhoea after antibiotics in an older inpatient ↓ Suspect C. difficile ↓ Organism forms spores ↓ Spores resist alcohol ↓ Soap and water handwashing
exam_trap: A, Alcohol-based gel — it is the default for most ward hand hygiene, but it is ineffective against C. difficile spores.
takeaway: When C. difficile is suspected, clean hands with soap and water, not alcohol gel.

stem:
A 68-year-old man in a single room on a surgical ward has had profuse watery diarrhoea since completing a course of co-amoxiclav. Testing for Clostridioides difficile is pending. The ward manager asks the infection prevention nurse what cleaning his room and commode need.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Routine daily cleaning with detergent only
options.B: Wiping his bedside locker and personal items only
options.C: Using air freshener to reduce odour
options.D: Cleaning the room and equipment with a sporicidal agent such as a chlorine-based product
options.E: No change to cleaning until the result confirms infection

correct_answer: D. Cleaning the room and equipment with a sporicidal agent such as a chlorine-based product
why_correct: C. difficile spores can survive on surfaces and equipment for months and are resistant to many standard detergents. Cleaning with a sporicidal agent, usually chlorine-based, reduces the environmental reservoir and transmission to other patients. This should start as soon as infection is suspected.
why_wrong: A. Detergent alone does not reliably destroy spores. B. Spores contaminate the whole environment, including toilets, commodes and frequently touched surfaces, not just personal items. C. Air freshener has no disinfectant effect. E. Delaying cleaning while awaiting results allows spores to accumulate and spread.
pearl: Shared equipment such as commodes should be dedicated to the patient where possible, and the room should have a terminal clean with a sporicidal product after discharge.
thinking: Diarrhoea after antibiotics ↓ Suspected C. difficile ↓ Spores persist on surfaces ↓ Detergents are not sporicidal ↓ Chlorine-based or other sporicidal cleaning
exam_trap: A, Routine detergent cleaning — it sounds adequate for a single room, but detergents do not kill C. difficile spores.
takeaway: Suspected C. difficile needs sporicidal environmental cleaning, not routine detergent alone.

stem:
On a busy medical admissions unit, a 52-year-old man who recently arrived from a country with high tuberculosis prevalence is being clerked. He has had a productive cough for two months, drenching sweats and loss of appetite, and his chest radiograph shows right upper lobe cavitation. Sputum samples have been sent but no results are back yet.

Where should he be nursed while awaiting results?

options.A: In a bay alongside other patients with respiratory infections
options.B: In an open bay using gloves and aprons for direct contact
options.C: In a protective isolation room to shield him from other patients' organisms
options.D: In a single side room with airborne (respiratory) precautions
options.E: In an open bay using standard precautions only until smear results return

correct_answer: D. In a single side room with airborne (respiratory) precautions
why_correct: Cavitating upper lobe disease with a chronic productive cough is highly suggestive of infectious pulmonary tuberculosis, which spreads by inhaled droplet nuclei. He should be placed in a single room, ideally with negative pressure or good ventilation, and staff should use respiratory protection as local policy requires. Isolation starts on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for confirmation.
why_wrong: A. Grouping him with other chest patients, who may be frail or immunocompromised, risks airborne spread. B. Gloves and aprons address contact spread and do nothing for airborne particles. C. Protective (reverse barrier) isolation is for immunosuppressed patients, not for containing an infectious one. E. Waiting for smear results in an open bay exposes other patients during the most infectious period.
pearl: Patients with suspected infectious pulmonary TB should not be nursed near immunocompromised patients, and suspected multidrug-resistant TB needs a negative-pressure room.
thinking: Chronic productive cough, sweats and weight loss ↓ Upper lobe cavitation on radiograph ↓ Probable infectious pulmonary TB ↓ Spread is airborne ↓ Single room with respiratory precautions from the outset
exam_trap: E, Standard precautions until smear results return — it seems proportionate to wait for proof, but airborne precautions should begin as soon as infectious TB is suspected.
takeaway: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs a single room with airborne precautions straight away.

stem:
A 31-year-old primary school teacher who is 16 weeks pregnant phones her GP surgery. Several children in her class have been off with a mild fever, and one returned today with bright red cheeks and a lacy rash on the arms. She wants to know which infection this is likely to be, as she is worried about the baby.

Which virus is most likely?

options.A: Measles virus
options.B: Rubella virus
options.C: Human herpesvirus 6
options.D: Varicella-zoster virus
options.E: Parvovirus B19

correct_answer: E. Parvovirus B19
why_correct: Bright red slapped-cheek erythema followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the limbs is typical of erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), caused by parvovirus B19. Children are often no longer infectious once the rash appears. In pregnancy, particularly before 20 weeks, infection can cause fetal anaemia and hydrops, so she should have serology checked.
why_wrong: A. Measles causes coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a maculopapular rash spreading from behind the ears. B. Rubella gives a fine pink macular rash with occipital lymphadenopathy, not slapped cheeks. C. Human herpesvirus 6 causes roseola, with high fever followed by a rash as the fever settles, mainly in infants. D. Varicella causes crops of itchy vesicles.
pearl: A pregnant woman exposed to a rash illness should have blood tested for parvovirus B19 and rubella (and measles if indicated); confirmed parvovirus infection before 20 weeks needs referral for fetal medicine monitoring.
thinking: Pregnant woman exposed to a rash illness ↓ Slapped cheeks then lacy limb rash ↓ Erythema infectiosum ↓ Parvovirus B19 ↓ Risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops
exam_trap: B, Rubella — it is the rash illness most associated with fetal harm, but the slapped-cheek pattern identifies parvovirus B19.
takeaway: A slapped-cheek rash means parvovirus B19, which can cause fetal hydrops in pregnancy.

stem:
At her booking appointment, a 27-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant tells the midwife that she likes her steak rare and helps her partner empty the litter tray of their two cats. She has read that one infection linked to these habits can damage the baby's eyes and brain.

Which infection is she most likely thinking of?

options.A: Listeriosis
options.B: Parvovirus B19 infection
options.C: Cytomegalovirus infection
options.D: Toxoplasmosis
options.E: Hepatitis E infection

correct_answer: D. Toxoplasmosis
why_correct: Toxoplasma gondii is acquired by eating undercooked or cured meat containing tissue cysts, or by ingesting oocysts from cat faeces, soil or unwashed vegetables. Primary infection in pregnancy can cross the placenta and cause chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcification. Advice is to eat well-cooked meat, wear gloves for gardening and avoid handling cat litter.
why_wrong: A. Listeria is linked to unpasteurised dairy, soft cheeses and pâté rather than cat faeces, and mainly causes miscarriage and neonatal sepsis. B. Parvovirus B19 spreads by respiratory secretions and causes fetal anaemia and hydrops. C. Cytomegalovirus is spread mainly via saliva and urine of young children, not cats or meat. E. Hepatitis E is linked to undercooked pork and causes severe maternal hepatitis rather than fetal brain and eye damage.
pearl: The classic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcification; routine antenatal screening for toxoplasmosis is not offered in the UK.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Rare meat and cat litter exposure ↓ Concern about fetal eyes and brain ↓ Matches Toxoplasma gondii ↓ Toxoplasmosis
exam_trap: A, Listeriosis — it is the other well-known food-related risk in pregnancy, but it is linked to dairy and chilled foods, not cat faeces.
takeaway: Undercooked meat and cat faeces in pregnancy point to toxoplasmosis.

stem:
Two children at the same nursery are diagnosed with acute hepatitis A after developing jaundice and dark urine. The local health protection team meets nursery staff to discuss how to stop further cases.

Which measure is most important in limiting spread in this setting?

options.A: Screening all staff for hepatitis B surface antigen
options.B: Thorough handwashing after nappy changes and toileting, and hygienic food preparation
options.C: Asking staff to wear surgical masks indoors
options.D: Stopping the sharing of toothbrushes and razors
options.E: Removing unpasteurised milk from the menu

correct_answer: B. Thorough handwashing after nappy changes and toileting, and hygienic food preparation
why_correct: Hepatitis A spreads by the faecal-oral route, and young children often have mild or no symptoms while shedding the virus. Careful handwashing with soap and water after toileting and nappy changes, and good hygiene in food handling, are the key measures. Vaccination of close contacts is also used by health protection teams to control outbreaks.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis B screening does not address a faecal-oral virus. C. Hepatitis A is not spread by the respiratory route, so masks do not help. D. Sharing toothbrushes and razors is a concern for blood-borne viruses such as hepatitis B and C. E. Unpasteurised milk is associated with organisms such as Listeria and Brucella rather than hepatitis A.
pearl: Hepatitis A is usually self-limiting and does not cause chronic infection; contacts can be protected with hepatitis A vaccine if given within 2 weeks of exposure.
thinking: Cluster of jaundice in a nursery ↓ Hepatitis A ↓ Faecal-oral transmission ↓ Young children often asymptomatic shedders ↓ Hand hygiene and safe food handling
exam_trap: D, Stopping the sharing of toothbrushes and razors — it is a familiar hepatitis prevention message, but it applies to blood-borne hepatitis B and C.
takeaway: Hepatitis A is faecal-oral, so hand and food hygiene are central to preventing spread.

stem:
A GP is reviewing preventive care for a 74-year-old man who has just moved into a nursing home. He has type 2 diabetes and heart failure. Last winter, an outbreak of fever, cough and muscle aches in the home led to two hospital admissions.

Which intervention will best reduce his risk of a similar illness this winter?

options.A: Taking a daily vitamin C supplement through the winter months
options.B: A single pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine dose repeated each autumn
options.C: Inactivated influenza vaccine every autumn
options.D: Low-dose amoxicillin taken daily from October to March
options.E: An annual chest X-ray to detect early lung infection

correct_answer: C. Inactivated influenza vaccine every autumn
why_correct: The outbreak described is typical of seasonal influenza. Under the UK national immunisation programme, adults aged 65 and over, care-home residents and people with chronic heart disease or diabetes are offered influenza vaccine every autumn, because circulating strains change and protection wanes. Vaccinating residents and staff reduces infections, outbreaks and hospital admissions.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin C has not been shown to prevent influenza. B. Pneumococcal vaccine protects against pneumococcal disease, not influenza, and is not given every year. D. Prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent a viral illness and drive antimicrobial resistance. E. Chest radiography has no preventive role.
pearl: The influenza vaccine is reformulated each year to match the strains expected to circulate, which is why it must be repeated annually.
thinking: Care-home resident with comorbidities ↓ Winter outbreak of fever, cough and myalgia ↓ Seasonal influenza ↓ Eligible under the national programme ↓ Annual influenza vaccination
exam_trap: B, Pneumococcal vaccine each autumn — it is also offered to older adults and protects against a winter chest infection, but it does not prevent influenza and is not an annual vaccine.
takeaway: Annual influenza vaccination is the main preventive measure for older and at-risk adults, including care-home residents.

stem:
A newly qualified nurse in a general practice treatment room tells a colleague that she only uses gloves, aprons and careful sharps disposal for patients known to have an infection such as hepatitis or HIV. Her colleague explains how standard infection control precautions should be applied.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: They are needed only for patients with a confirmed or suspected infection
options.B: They apply to hospital wards but not to community clinics
options.C: They make additional transmission-based precautions unnecessary
options.D: They apply to every patient at all times, with PPE chosen according to the task
options.E: They are only required during invasive or surgical procedures

correct_answer: D. They apply to every patient at all times, with PPE chosen according to the task
why_correct: Standard infection control precautions, such as hand hygiene, appropriate PPE, safe sharps handling and management of blood and body fluids, apply to all patients in all settings. Infection status is often unknown, so every patient is treated as a potential source. The type of PPE is chosen according to the anticipated exposure for each task.
why_wrong: A. Many people with blood-borne viruses are undiagnosed, so restricting precautions to known cases leaves staff and patients at risk. B. They apply equally in primary care, community and hospital settings. C. Transmission-based precautions, such as airborne or contact isolation, are added on top when a specific infection is suspected. E. They apply to all care activities, including routine examination and specimen handling.
pearl: Transmission-based precautions (contact, droplet or airborne) are always used in addition to, never instead of, standard precautions.
thinking: Nurse uses precautions only for known infection ↓ Infection status is often unknown ↓ Standard precautions are universal ↓ PPE matched to the task ↓ Apply to every patient in every setting
exam_trap: A, Only for known or suspected infection — it seems efficient, but undiagnosed infection is common, which is why precautions are universal.
takeaway: Standard precautions apply to every patient, every time, in every care setting.

stem:
During an infection prevention audit on a respiratory ward, a junior doctor is observed cleaning his hands only after he finishes examining each patient. He explains that he does this to avoid carrying organisms to the next person.

Which approach to hand hygiene should he adopt?

options.A: Clean hands after each patient only, as he is already doing
options.B: Clean hands only when they look visibly soiled
options.C: Clean hands at the beginning and end of the shift and before meals
options.D: Clean hands before and after touching a patient, before aseptic tasks, after body-fluid exposure and after touching the patient's surroundings
options.E: Clean hands before putting on gloves, but not after taking them off

correct_answer: D. Clean hands before and after touching a patient, before aseptic tasks, after body-fluid exposure and after touching the patient's surroundings
why_correct: The WHO five moments for hand hygiene are before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body-fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient and after touching the patient's surroundings. Cleaning hands before contact protects the patient from organisms picked up elsewhere, including from surfaces. Cleaning only afterwards leaves the patient unprotected.
why_wrong: A. Cleaning only after contact protects the next patient but not the one being examined. B. Hands can carry pathogens while looking clean. C. Hand hygiene must happen at the point of care around each contact, not at fixed times of day. E. Hands become contaminated through glove defects and during removal, so hand hygiene is needed after taking gloves off.
pearl: Hand hygiene is the single most effective measure for preventing healthcare-associated infection, and gloves never replace it.
thinking: Doctor cleans hands after contact only ↓ Patient is unprotected from organisms on his hands ↓ Hand hygiene is needed at defined moments ↓ WHO five moments ↓ Before and after contact plus other key moments
exam_trap: A, After each patient only — it seems logical because it protects the next person, but the current patient also needs protecting before contact.
takeaway: Hand hygiene is needed before and after patient contact and at the other WHO key moments.

stem:
A foundation doctor in the emergency department is about to insert an arterial line in an agitated, ventilated patient with a large scalp wound that is still bleeding. She asks the nurse in charge how to decide what personal protective equipment to wear.

What should guide her choice?

options.A: The doctor's own comfort and preference
options.B: An assessment of the likely exposure to blood and body fluids during the task
options.C: Whether the patient has a known infection recorded in the notes
options.D: The patient's age and frailty
options.E: The number of procedures she has already performed that shift

correct_answer: B. An assessment of the likely exposure to blood and body fluids during the task
why_correct: Under standard infection control precautions, PPE is selected by assessing the risk of exposure to blood, body fluids, mucous membranes or non-intact skin during the specific task. An arterial line in an agitated patient carries a risk of splashes, so gloves, an apron or gown and eye or face protection are appropriate. The decision is based on the task, not on whether infection is already known.
why_wrong: A. Personal preference is not a safe basis for protection. C. Infection status is frequently unknown, so PPE is chosen by exposure risk rather than diagnosis. D. Age and frailty do not alter the risk of blood exposure to the clinician. E. The number of earlier procedures has no bearing on exposure risk.
pearl: Eye and face protection should be worn whenever there is a risk of blood or body fluid splashing, for example during arterial procedures or wound irrigation.
thinking: Procedure with bleeding and arterial access ↓ Possible splash exposure ↓ Infection status unknown ↓ Standard precautions use a task risk assessment ↓ PPE matched to anticipated exposure
exam_trap: C, Known infection in the notes — it seems sensible to escalate PPE for known infection, but most blood-borne infection is undiagnosed, so the task risk decides.
takeaway: PPE is chosen by assessing the anticipated exposure risk of the task, not by the patient's known diagnosis.

stem:
A 34-year-old man attends a drug and alcohol service for a health check. He has injected heroin intermittently for several years and also has tattoos done professionally, plays football in a team, uses a public gym and lives with a partner who shares meals with him.

Which activity puts him at the greatest risk of acquiring hepatitis C?

options.A: Sharing meals and cutlery with his partner
options.B: Using the showers and pool at a public gym
options.C: Sharing needles, syringes or other injecting equipment
options.D: Close body contact during football matches
options.E: Kissing his partner

correct_answer: C. Sharing needles, syringes or other injecting equipment
why_correct: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne virus, and sharing needles, syringes, spoons, filters or water when injecting is the main route of transmission in the UK. Anyone who has ever injected drugs should be offered testing. Sexual and household transmission are uncommon.
why_wrong: A. Sharing food and cutlery does not transmit hepatitis C. B. Swimming pools and showers are not a route of spread. D. Ordinary sporting contact without blood exposure is not a recognised route. E. Kissing is not a recognised route of transmission.
pearl: Hepatitis C is now curable in most people with 8 to 12 weeks of direct-acting antiviral treatment, so testing people who inject drugs is high value.
thinking: Man who injects drugs ↓ Hepatitis C is blood-borne ↓ Shared injecting equipment carries blood ↓ Casual and household contact do not ↓ Injecting equipment is the main risk
exam_trap: A, Sharing meals and cutlery — household contact feels risky, but hepatitis C needs blood exposure and is not spread through food.
takeaway: Sharing injecting equipment is the main route of hepatitis C transmission.

stem:
Before starting a TNF-alpha inhibitor for rheumatoid arthritis, a 46-year-old woman has screening tests. Her interferon-gamma release assay is positive, but she feels well, has no cough, fever or weight loss, and her chest radiograph is clear.

What best describes her tuberculosis status?

options.A: Miliary tuberculosis
options.B: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis
options.C: Active pulmonary tuberculosis
options.D: Latent tuberculosis infection
options.E: Tuberculous lymphadenitis

correct_answer: D. Latent tuberculosis infection
why_correct: A positive interferon-gamma release assay shows immune sensitisation to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. With no symptoms and a normal chest radiograph, there is no evidence of active disease, so this is latent infection. She is not infectious, but treatment of latent infection is recommended before biological therapy because immunosuppression increases the risk of reactivation.
why_wrong: A. Miliary TB is disseminated active disease with systemic illness and a characteristic radiograph. B. Multidrug resistance describes drug susceptibility, which cannot be assessed from a screening test and does not describe this state. C. Active pulmonary TB would usually cause symptoms and radiographic changes. E. Tuberculous lymphadenitis is active extrapulmonary disease with enlarged nodes.
pearl: Latent TB is not infectious and does not need isolation; treatment is typically 3 months of isoniazid with rifampicin or 6 months of isoniazid.
thinking: Positive IGRA ↓ No symptoms ↓ Normal chest radiograph ↓ No evidence of active disease ↓ Latent TB infection
exam_trap: C, Active pulmonary tuberculosis — a positive TB test is easily taken as disease, but an IGRA only shows infection, not whether it is active.
takeaway: A positive TB immune test with no symptoms and a clear chest radiograph indicates latent infection.

stem:
A 23-year-old woman shared a small, poorly ventilated flat for several months with a friend who has just been diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. She asks the TB nurse how she might have caught it if her own screening is positive.

By what route is pulmonary tuberculosis usually spread?

options.A: Swallowing contaminated water
options.B: Faecal-oral spread on unwashed hands
options.C: Bites from insects such as mosquitoes
options.D: Inhaling airborne droplet nuclei from an infectious person's cough
options.E: Eating food prepared by the infected person

correct_answer: D. Inhaling airborne droplet nuclei from an infectious person's cough
why_correct: Pulmonary TB spreads when a person with infectious lung disease coughs, sneezes or speaks, releasing tiny droplet nuclei containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis that stay suspended in the air and are inhaled by others. Prolonged close contact in a shared, poorly ventilated space is the highest-risk situation. Household contacts are therefore prioritised for screening.
why_wrong: A. Contaminated water is not a route for pulmonary TB. B. TB is not spread faecal-orally; that route is typical of hepatitis A and enteric infections. C. TB is not carried by insects. E. Food handled by an infected person does not transmit pulmonary TB; Mycobacterium bovis in unpasteurised milk is a different, now rare, route.
pearl: Smear-positive pulmonary disease is the most infectious form of TB, and household contacts are screened as a priority.
thinking: Prolonged contact in a shared flat ↓ Index case has smear-positive lung disease ↓ Organism expelled by coughing ↓ Droplet nuclei remain airborne ↓ Inhalation is the route
exam_trap: E, Food prepared by the infected person — sharing a home suggests food spread, but pulmonary TB is transmitted through the air.
takeaway: Pulmonary TB is spread by inhaling airborne droplet nuclei from someone with infectious lung disease.

stem:
An 18-year-old university fresher is admitted with meningococcal septicaemia. The health protection team arranges antibiotic prophylaxis for her flatmates and boyfriend but not for the classmates in her lecture group. Her worried mother asks how the infection spreads.

Which route of transmission explains this approach?

options.A: Bites from infected insects
options.B: Eating contaminated food from a shared kitchen
options.C: Faecal-oral spread from shared toilets
options.D: Respiratory droplets and secretions during prolonged close contact
options.E: Contact with contaminated soil

correct_answer: D. Respiratory droplets and secretions during prolonged close contact
why_correct: Neisseria meningitidis colonises the nasopharynx and spreads through respiratory droplets and direct contact with secretions, for example through kissing or living in the same household. Spread therefore needs prolonged close contact, which is why prophylaxis targets household and intimate contacts rather than casual contacts.
why_wrong: A. Meningococcus is not spread by insects. B. Contaminated food is not a route of transmission. C. It is not spread by the faecal-oral route. E. Soil is not a reservoir; humans are the only natural host.
pearl: Close contacts of a case of invasive meningococcal disease are offered a single dose of ciprofloxacin as prophylaxis, ideally within 24 hours of diagnosis.
thinking: Invasive meningococcal disease ↓ Organism carried in the nasopharynx ↓ Spread by droplets and secretions ↓ Needs prolonged close contact ↓ Prophylaxis for household and intimate contacts only
exam_trap: B, Contaminated food from a shared kitchen — flatmates share a kitchen, which makes food spread seem plausible, but transmission is via respiratory secretions.
takeaway: Meningococcal infection spreads by respiratory droplets and secretions during close contact.

stem:
A 40-year-old man who recently returned from a stay in a region with an ongoing diphtheria outbreak develops a sore throat, low-grade fever and a grey membrane over the tonsils. Public health staff begin tracing the people he has been near.

By what route is this infection most likely to have spread to him?

options.A: Respiratory droplets from an infected person
options.B: Faecal-oral spread from contaminated water
options.C: Mosquito bites
options.D: Sexual contact only
options.E: Contact with soil only

correct_answer: A. Respiratory droplets from an infected person
why_correct: Respiratory diphtheria, caused by toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae, spreads mainly by respiratory droplets and close contact with secretions from infected people or carriers. The grey adherent pharyngeal membrane after travel to an outbreak area is characteristic. Close contacts need assessment, swabbing, antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccination as advised by public health.
why_wrong: B. Diphtheria is not spread through contaminated water. C. It is not transmitted by mosquitoes. D. Sexual contact is not a typical route. E. Soil is not the source of respiratory diphtheria; cutaneous diphtheria spreads through contact with skin lesions.
pearl: Suspected diphtheria is a notifiable disease and is treated urgently with diphtheria antitoxin plus antibiotics; the toxin can cause myocarditis and neuropathy.
thinking: Recent travel to an outbreak area ↓ Sore throat with grey pharyngeal membrane ↓ Respiratory diphtheria ↓ Spread by droplets and secretions ↓ Close contacts need tracing
exam_trap: E, Contact with soil only — it can be confused with tetanus, another toxin-mediated vaccine-preventable infection, but respiratory diphtheria spreads person to person by droplets.
takeaway: Respiratory diphtheria spreads through respiratory droplets and close contact with infected secretions.

stem:
Two days after a 63-year-old woman was admitted for a planned laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the laboratory reports that one of two sets of blood cultures, taken from separate sites during a brief temperature spike on the night of surgery, has grown coagulase-negative staphylococci. She has no prosthetic heart valve, implanted device or central venous line, her temperature settled within hours, and she is now eating and mobilising. Repeat cultures show no growth.

What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Infective endocarditis requiring echocardiography
options.B: Occult bacteraemia requiring broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
options.C: Early septic shock requiring fluid resuscitation
options.D: Bacterial meningitis requiring lumbar puncture
options.E: Contamination of the blood culture by skin organisms

correct_answer: E. Contamination of the blood culture by skin organisms
why_correct: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are normal skin flora and a common contaminant introduced when blood cultures are taken. Growth in only one set, in a patient who is clinically well and has negative repeat cultures, makes contamination the most likely explanation. True infection is more likely with multiple positive sets or an indwelling line or implanted prosthetic material.
why_wrong: A. Endocarditis typically gives persistently positive cultures in several sets. B. Starting antibiotics for a probable contaminant in a well patient is unnecessary and promotes resistance. C. She is clinically well, so septic shock is not present. D. Nothing suggests meningitis, and a single blood culture does not diagnose it.
pearl: Taking two sets of blood cultures from separate sites with careful skin antisepsis helps distinguish true bacteraemia from contamination.
thinking: Skin organism in one of two sets ↓ Patient now well ↓ Repeat cultures negative ↓ No line, valve or implanted device ↓ Most likely contamination
exam_trap: B, Occult bacteraemia needing broad-spectrum antibiotics — treating every positive culture feels safe, but a single probable contaminant in a well patient does not need antibiotics.
takeaway: A single culture growing a skin organism in a well patient with negative repeats is most likely contamination.
notes: Reviewer fix: Removed new knee prosthesis (CoNS is a true prosthetic-joint pathogen, undermining the contamination key); now laparoscopic cholecystectomy, 'one of two sets from separate sites' instead of one bottle; thinking/why_correct aligned

stem:
A 29-year-old man feels well but was told by the blood donation service that a routine screen of his donation was reactive for HBsAg. His GP sends a further sample nine months later, and the same marker is again detected.

Which interpretation fits these findings?

options.A: Chronic hepatitis B infection
options.B: Immunity following hepatitis B vaccination
options.C: Past hepatitis B infection that has cleared
options.D: Acute hepatitis A infection
options.E: Previous hepatitis C infection

correct_answer: A. Chronic hepatitis B infection
why_correct: Hepatitis B surface antigen is a marker of current infection. When it persists for longer than 6 months, the infection is defined as chronic. He needs referral to a specialist service for assessment of viral load, e-antigen status and liver disease, and his close contacts should be offered testing and vaccination.
why_wrong: B. Vaccination produces anti-HBs antibody only, not surface antigen. C. Cleared infection is marked by loss of surface antigen with anti-HBc and usually anti-HBs. D. Hepatitis A is a different virus and does not produce hepatitis B surface antigen. E. Hepatitis C status is assessed by its own antibody and RNA tests.
pearl: Persistence of HBsAg for more than 6 months defines chronic hepatitis B; the risk of chronicity is highest when infection is acquired at birth or in early childhood.
thinking: HBsAg positive on first test ↓ Still positive nine months later ↓ HBsAg indicates current infection ↓ Persistence over 6 months ↓ Chronic hepatitis B
exam_trap: C, Past infection that has cleared — he feels well, which suggests resolution, but cleared infection requires loss of surface antigen.
takeaway: Hepatitis B surface antigen persisting beyond 6 months means chronic hepatitis B infection.
